title: Galactic Encounters
subtitle: When galaxies meet across cosmic time
description: Interactive exhibit on galaxy interactions: tidal forces, tails and bridges, stars versus gas, major and minor mergers, observed systems, and the uncertain future of the Milky Way and Andromeda.
source_note: Scientific outreach. Encounter and tidal labs are ILLUSTRATIVE. Observed systems cite Hubble/ESA/NASA media. Milky Way–Andromeda content is FUTURE PREDICTION / SIMULATION and model-dependent—not a fixed calendar date.
illustrative_disclaimer: ILLUSTRATIVE GALAXY ENCOUNTER — educational sketches, not N-body trajectories of a specific observed pair unless separately labeled.

classification_legend.future_prediction: Forward model of a system not yet observed at that epoch

science.gravity: Galaxies influence one another primarily through gravity acting across tens to hundreds of thousands of light-years. Stars within each galaxy remain widely separated.
science.stars_miss: Even when disks overlap, the odds that two individual stars collide head-on are tiny—stellar separations are enormous compared with stellar sizes.
science.gas_collides: Interstellar gas and dust interact strongly: clouds can compress, shock, and cool, often fueling new star formation. Not every encounter produces the same starburst.
science.tides: Differential gravity across a galaxy stretches material—the near side feels a stronger pull than the far side—drawing out tidal tails and bridges over long times.
science.timescales: Close passages and mergers unfold over hundreds of millions to billions of years. A first flyby does not instantly finish a merger.
science.major_minor: Major mergers involve comparable masses and can scramble disks globally. Minor mergers embed smaller galaxies into larger ones, often leaving streams or shells.
science.dark_matter: Extended dark-matter halos dominate the mass budget and strongly shape encounter orbits and dynamical friction.
science.remnants: Outcomes vary: disturbed disks, elliptical-like remnants, rebuilt gas-rich disks, shells/streams, central starbursts, or AGN fueling if gas reaches the nucleus.
science.mw_m31: Andromeda shows blueshift toward the Milky Way, so a future Local Group encounter is expected on billion-year timescales. Exact timing, impact parameter, and remnant morphology remain model-dependent. Recent dynamical studies (including Magellanic Cloud mass/orbit effects) revise encounter likelihood and timing—do not treat any single 'collision in X billion years' figure as settled fact. This section is FUTURE PREDICTION / SIMULATION, not a calendar event.

encounter_lab.label: ILLUSTRATIVE GALAXY ENCOUNTER
encounter_lab.disclaimer: Conceptual stages only—not calibrated N-body particles of Antennae, Mice, or M51.

stages.label: Approach
stages.caption: Two galaxies fall toward each other under mutual gravity.

stages.label: First passage
stages.caption: Closest approach begins to distort disks; bridges may start.

stages.label: Tidal distortion
stages.caption: Differential gravity warps disks and pulls material outward.

stages.label: Tails and bridges
stages.caption: Extended tidal tails and bridges become prominent.

stages.label: Later passages
stages.caption: Orbital energy drains; repeated encounters can deepen the interaction.

stages.label: Merger / remnant
stages.caption: If bound, systems may coalesce into a disturbed or elliptical-like remnant over Gyr.

orientations.label: Prograde-style
orientations.note: Disk spins roughly aligned with the encounter orbit—often stronger tidal response.

orientations.label: Retrograde-style
orientations.note: Opposite sense of rotation—often milder disk response for the same path.

tidal_lab.label: GALAXY-SCALE TIDAL STRETCH
tidal_lab.disclaimer: Shows differential gravity across a disk companion. Distinct from black-hole horizon tides—here the perturber is another galaxy.
tidal_lab.caption: Near-side material feels a stronger pull than the far side; the disk stretches into tails over long timescales.

modes.label: Stars
modes.caption: Collisionless stellar orbits mostly pass through; direct star–star impacts are rare.

modes.label: Gas
modes.caption: Gas clouds can collide, shock, and compress—helping trigger star formation and bright UV/IR regions.

modes.label: Together
modes.caption: Stars stream while gas piles up—why overlapping galaxies can look stormy without stellar pile-ups.

modes.label: Major merger
modes.caption: Roughly comparable masses: strong global disruption is common; disks may be scrambled before a remnant settles.

modes.label: Minor merger
modes.caption: A much smaller galaxy is accreted: the large disk often survives with streams, shells, or a thickened halo.

future_mw_m31.label: FUTURE PREDICTION / SIMULATION
future_mw_m31.disclaimer: FUTURE PREDICTION / SIMULATION — model-dependent. Observed: Andromeda approaches (blueshift). Not observed: the future merger geometry. Do not hard-code a single collision year. Orbit mass models (Milky Way, M31, Magellanic Clouds) continue to update timing and whether a direct head-on merger is favored. Simulation images are not photographs of our future sky.
points: Andromeda’s spectrum shows approach (blueshift) relative to the Milky Way.
Billion-year timescales are the relevant teaching frame—not human history.
Simulations explore families of outcomes; they are not photographs of our future sky.
Uncertainty is scientifically honest: refine orbits, still revise timing and morphology.

narration.motion: Galaxies are not lonely islands. Gravity reaches across millions of light-years and slowly rearranges their shapes.
narration.tides: Tidal forces stretch a galaxy because the near side feels a stronger pull than the far side. Over long ages, that stretch becomes tails and bridges.
narration.tails: Tidal tails and bridges are rivers of stars and gas pulled outward during close passages—billboards of past encounters.
narration.stars_gas: Stars usually miss each other, but gas clouds can slam together and light new stars. That is why interacting galaxies often look stormy.
narration.antennae: The Antennae are a classic merger in progress: overlapping disks, furious star formation, and long tidal antennae.
narration.whirlpool: The Whirlpool Galaxy shows how a companion can help sculpt spiral structure while the pair continues to interact.
narration.major_minor: Major mergers scramble peers; minor mergers let a large galaxy grow by eating smaller ones, often leaving stellar streams.
narration.remnants: There is no single ending. Remnants may look elliptical-like, rebuild disks, host starbursts, or feed a central black hole.
narration.mw_m31: Andromeda approaches the Milky Way on cosmic timescales. Simulations explore possible futures, but exact timing and geometry remain model-dependent—no single collision date is certain.
narration.closing: Galaxies grow by encounter. Watching tails, bridges, and starbursts, we read gravity’s long conversation across the sky.
